item.title: Osaka Cooking Class & Food Tour Guide: Eat & Cook Like a Local
item.description: Osaka calls itself “the nation’s kitchen” and lives by the motto kuidaore — “eat until you drop.” So there’s no better city to dive into Japanese food hands-on, whether by learning to flip your own takoyaki and griddle okonomiyaki, or by following a local guide through the neon of Dotonbori and the stalls of Kuromon on a food tour. Both turn Osaka’s famous street food from something you eat into something you understand — and they’re sociable, delicious, and genuinely fun.

item.title: Osaka Takoyaki Cooking Class Guide: Flip Your Own Octopus Balls
item.description: Eating takoyaki in Osaka is essential — but making it is a different kind of fun. The mesmerising flick-and-turn that shapes runny batter into perfect crisp spheres is genuinely tricky, and a takoyaki-making class lets you try it yourself on a real dimpled pan, with a local teacher guiding your wrist. It’s hands-on, hilarious, and you eat your wonky-but-delicious results at the end — one of Osaka’s most enjoyable and very on-brand experiences for foodies, couples, and families.

item.title: Osaka Takoyaki Guide: The City's Soul Food, Explained
item.description: If Osaka has one defining food, it’s takoyaki — piping-hot, golden balls of savoury batter with a chunk of octopus inside, brushed with sweet-savoury sauce, mayonnaise, and a flurry of dancing bonito flakes. Born in Osaka in the 1930s, takoyaki is the city’s ultimate street snack: cooked on dimpled iron griddles in a hypnotic flipping motion, sold from stalls and specialist shops on nearly every corner of Minami. Crisp outside, molten and creamy inside, it’s Osaka soul food at its purest.

item.title: Osaka Food Guide: Takoyaki, Kushikatsu, Kuidaore & Where Locals Actually Eat
item.description: Osaka’s relationship with food is unlike any other Japanese city. The phrase kuidaore (食い倒れ — “eat until you drop”) is both the city’s motto and a description of actual behaviour: Osaka residents spend a higher percentage of household income on food than any other city in Japan, and the city’s food culture is the most democratic in the country — great meals are found in market stalls and basement counters as readily as in restaurant dining rooms.
